bluf.text: Japan is in its biggest military build-up since 1945: 2% of GDP reached two years early, its first long-range counterstrike missiles fielded in 2026, all three services under one joint command, and ground forces shifting to the Southwest Islands.

key_facts.text: About 220,000 uniformed personnel against an authorised 247,154 (89%, March 2025). The Ground Self-Defense Force has about 131,000 of them.

The FY2026 defence budget is a record ¥9.04 trillion (about US$58B) including US-realignment costs. With Coast Guard and other 'related' spending it reaches ¥10.6 trillion, which Japan counts as 1.9% of GDP (on its FY2022 base). On a current-GDP basis it is nearer 1.5%.

The 2022 strategy documents ended Japan's reliance on the US for all strike: they adopted 'counterstrike' with stand-off missiles and set the doubling of spending. PM Takaichi Sanae's government is rewriting all three documents for cabinet approval by the end of 2026.

Counterstrike is now real. On 31 March 2026 the GSDF fielded the Type 25 anti-ship missile (about 1,000 km) at Camp Kengun and the Type 25 hyper-velocity glide weapon at Camp Fuji. The destroyer Chokai fired Japan's first Tomahawk on 29 July 2026.

Since 24 March 2025 the Japan Joint Operations Command (JJOC) has commanded the three services in operations; Adm. Tawara Tateki took command on 23 March 2026. The US began upgrading US Forces Japan to a joint force headquarters to work with it.

snapshot.so_what_saf: Japan faces the SAF's problems at larger scale: fewer recruits, the move to unmanned systems and long-range fires, and joint command of island and maritime defence. Its methods matter more to us than its equipment.

summary.text: The JSDF has three services under the Joint Staff, and since March 2025 the JJOC commands them in operations. The Ground Self-Defense Force is the largest: about 131,000 personnel in the Ground Component Command and five regional armies, with 9 divisions, 6 combined brigades and national units (airborne, amphibious, helicopter, special forces). Its weight is moving from heavy armour in Hokkaido to anti-ship missiles, amphibious forces, electronic warfare and island garrisons in Kyushu and the Southwest Islands.

active_personnel.text: As of 31 March 2025: 220,252 actual against 247,154 authorised (89.1%). GSDF 131,293 of 149,767 (87.7%); MSDF 41,818 of 45,452 (92.0%); ASDF 42,608 of 47,007 (90.6%); Joint Staff and others 4,533 of 4,928. Hiring rose 14.9% to 11,177 in FY2025.

local.text: ¥9.0353 trillion in the initial FY2026 budget, a record. This includes SACO-related and US Forces realignment costs (e.g. ¥127B for the carrier-aircraft training facility on Mageshima). Excluding them it is ¥8.8093 trillion, up 3.9% on FY2025. The cabinet approved it on 26 December 2025.

usd.text: About US$58B at December 2025 rates (about ¥156/$), as reported by AP and Al Jazeera. At the roughly ¥160/$ implied by USNI's August 2026 conversion of the FY2027 request it is about US$56.5B (our arithmetic).

pct_gdp.text: Two measures. (1) The core MOD budget (¥9.04T) is about 1.3% of current GDP (our estimate). (2) Japan's official 'defence and related' measure adds Coast Guard, defence-relevant R&D and public infrastructure: ¥10.6T in FY2026, which Japan calls 1.9% of FY2022 GDP (the base it uses) and is about 1.5% of projected FY2026 GDP. The 2% goal (about ¥11T), originally set for FY2027, was declared met in FY2025 through a ¥1.1T defence top-up in the supplementary budget. No new target is set yet: the LDP's June 2026 proposal cited countries aiming at 3-3.5% without fixing a number, Washington has urged 3.5%, and the revised documents due by end-2026 are where any new goal would appear.

notes.text: The ¥43 trillion Defense Buildup Program (FY2023-2027) ends next year. The FY2027 request of ¥8.89T is only 0.9% above FY2026 and is expected to grow once the documents are revised. Watch the size of the successor five-year envelope.

The weak yen erodes buying power for US-sourced items (F-35, Tomahawk, MQ-9B). The yen's slide after the plan was set already forced aircraft cuts in 2024, and the rate was about ¥160/$ in August 2026.

Funding has begun: a 4% corporate surtax from April 2026, staged tobacco increases and an income-tax surcharge from January 2027. People, not money, are the binding limit. Hiring recovered to 11,177 in FY2025 but still missed target, and MOD expects the recruitable population to fall by about 30% between FY2024 and FY2045.

FY2026 (Apr 2026 to Mar 2027) initial defence-related budget is ¥9,035.3bn, including SACO and US-forces realignment costs (+3.8%; ¥8,809.3bn excluding them). It was enacted on 7 Apr 2026. Converted at about ¥156/US$, the rate implied by Bloomberg's ¥9.04tn = $57.9bn at cabinet approval (26 Dec 2025); Anadolu's April 2026 conversion gives about $56.5bn. This is a fiscal-year budget, not a SIPRI calendar-year figure. No % of GDP is shown: Japan's wider '2%' measure adds other outlays and supplementary budgets.

posture.text: Japan judges its environment the most severe since 1945, with China the main concern ahead of North Korea and Russia; the ASDF flew 595 scrambles in FY2025 (366 against Chinese aircraft, 214 against Russian). Since 2022 it has moved from a pure 'shield' that relied on US strike power to a force that can also hit back, defend the Southwest Islands and sustain a long fight, closely integrated with US forces.

doctrine.text: The three security documents of 16 December 2022 are the NSS (the first revision in nine years), the National Defense Strategy (replacing the NDPG) and the Defense Buildup Program. They call the environment 'as severe and complex as it has ever been since the end of WWII', adopt counterstrike capabilities and set defence and related spending at 2% of GDP.

The NDS names seven capability fields: stand-off defence, integrated air and missile defence, unmanned defence, cross-domain operations (space, cyber, electromagnetic), command and control with intelligence, mobile deployment with civil protection, and sustainability and resiliency.
Joint operations: the JJOC (March 2025) gives Japan a single operational commander for the first time, and is the counterpart for a US Forces Japan headquarters that is being upgraded in phases.

Southwest Islands defence means distributed island garrisons with anti-ship missiles, electronic warfare and an amphibious brigade, backed by rapid-deployment divisions from Kyushu. Keen Sword 2026 rehearses this as multi-island sea denial alongside US Marine anti-ship units.

programmes.text: Stand-off defence: about ¥970B in FY2026, including ¥177B for upgraded Type 12 (now Type 25) missiles. The Type 25 anti-ship missile and glide weapon were fielded in March 2026, and 400 Tomahawks (200 Block IV, 200 Block V) are due in FY2025-2027.
SHIELD: ¥100.1B in FY2026 for a layered coastal defence of air, surface and undersea drones meant to blunt an invasion force, due in FY2027 (by March 2028). The August 2025 request was ¥128.7B.

Southwest build-up: the 15th Brigade becomes a division within FY2026, electronic warfare units go to Ishigaki and Yonaguni, and supply arrangements in the region are being strengthened (Defense of Japan 2026).

current.text: Type 25 surface-to-ship missile (upgraded Type 12, about 1,000 km against about 200 km before) with the 5th Surface-to-Ship Missile Regiment at Camp Kengun since 31 March 2026. The Type 25 hyper-velocity gliding projectile is at Camp Fuji; its launcher was first shown publicly at a live-fire exercise in June 2026.

A coastal anti-ship missile network across the Ryukyus and Kyushu. It includes the 7th Regiment on Okinawa (2024) and the 8th Regiment at Yufuin (March 2025, about 300 personnel, three batteries) under the 2nd Artillery Brigade.

Tomahawk: deliveries began by March 2026, the destroyer Chokai completed modifications and fired the first round on 29 July 2026, and Japan plans to arm its Aegis destroyers (Kongo, Atago and Maya classes) with up to 400 missiles.
F-35: 147 on order (105 F-35A, 42 F-35B). The first three F-35Bs arrived at Nyutabaru on 7 August 2025, flight training began on 4 November 2025, and eight were planned by March 2026.
Amphibious Rapid Deployment Brigade at Sasebo with three amphibious regiments, Japan's force for retaking islands.

Electronic warfare and cyber: the GSDF Electronic Operations Unit (about 180 personnel, 2022) directs EW units across Kyushu and Okinawa. From 1 October 2026 the SDF, alongside police, may access and neutralise servers behind serious cyberattacks.

emerging.text: More long-range strike: the FY2027 request includes about US$1B for hypersonic missiles and ground equipment, and Tomahawk will spread across the Aegis destroyer fleet after Chokai.

Two Aegis System Equipped Vessels (ASEV) with SPY-7 radar for missile defence. Keels were laid in July 2025 (MHI Nagasaki) and February 2026 (JMU Yokohama). First launch is planned for FY2026, with commissioning in March 2028 and March 2029.

GCAP sixth-generation fighter with the UK and Italy. On 3 July 2026 GIGO signed the full design-and-development contract (to end-2027, about GBP4.6B) with Edgewing (BAE Systems, Leonardo, JAIEC). Service entry is targeted from 2035.
Unmanned systems at scale: SHIELD coastal drone defence (¥100.1B in FY2026), five wide-area surveillance UAVs (¥11.1B), and 17 MQ-9B SeaGuardians (about US$1.8B) in the FY2027 request.
AI, space and cyber are named priorities in the FY2027 request. Active cyber defence operations began on 1 October 2026 under a law passed in May 2025.

bio.text: Career politician who has held the House of Representatives seat for Kanagawa's 11th district since 2009, after graduate study at Columbia University and a research post at CSIS in Washington. He was Minister of the Environment (2019–2021), chaired the House Committee on Security (2024) and was Minister of Agriculture (May–Oct 2025). He ran twice for the LDP presidency and lost the 2025 run-off to Takaichi Sanae, who made him Minister of Defense on 21 Oct 2025. He kept the post in the February 2026 second Takaichi cabinet and the September 2026 reshuffle, and is driving an early revision of Japan's three strategic documents and a push on drones and unmanned systems.

positions.text: Press conference, 20 Feb 2026: his top priorities are protecting Japanese lives and livelihoods, defending Japan's territory, airspace and waters, and looking after SDF personnel and their families. He has been instructed to revise the three strategic documents by the end of 2026, ahead of schedule, together with the guidelines on defence equipment transfers.

Shangri-La Dialogue, 31 May 2026: rejected China's 'new militarism' label by contrasting Japan with 'a country' holding a huge nuclear arsenal and strategic bombers. He said Japan opposes unilateral changes to the status quo by force or coercion, and that 'Japan's door to dialogue is always open'.

On being retained in the September 2026 reshuffle, he said the second year calls for more speed and intensity than the first, not mere continuity. In a call with US Secretary Hegseth (18 Sep 2026) he stressed a strong sense of urgency on the document revision and on transforming Japan's defence capabilities.

Drones: on 9 Oct 2026 he announced a contract with Ukraine's SkyFall for interceptor drones, Japan's first such purchase from Ukraine (quantity and value undisclosed). He singled out Ukraine's ability to field improved drone systems every two to three weeks.
December 2025: called the Chinese J-15 radar lock-ons on ASDF F-15s near Okinawa a dangerous act going beyond what safe aircraft operations require.

hooks.text: At SLD 2026 (31 May) he and Minister Chan Chun Sing agreed to meet regularly, to pursue defence equipment and technology cooperation under the bilateral transfer agreement, and to use the JMOD–MINDEF Policy Talks working groups. He framed this under the Strategic Partnership agreed at the March 2026 summit. These agreed follow-ups give the SAF a ready-made agenda with his office.

Minister-level rapport is already warm: Chan hosted him at Gardens by the Bay the night before their SLD meeting. 2026 is the 60th anniversary of Singapore–Japan diplomatic relations, which makes an easy opener.

He is pressing hard on drones and unmanned systems, including Japan's first purchase of Ukrainian interceptor drones. Counter-UAS and fast drone procurement give a professional topic where the SAF has views to trade.

Japan is rewriting its three strategic documents by end-2026, and he has said the revision matters for the whole region. A Singapore and Southeast Asian perspective offered through policy channels before the drafts close is timely and low-cost.

bio.text: F-15 fighter pilot from Tarumizu, Kagoshima, who graduated from the National Defense Academy in 1987 and spent much of his career in ASDF and Joint Staff defence planning. He commanded the 5th Air Wing (2012) and Air Defense Command (2020) and was Chief of Staff, ASDF from March 2023. On 1 Aug 2025 he became the 8th Chief of Staff, Joint Staff, Japan's top uniformed officer, working alongside the new Joint Operations Command. He has been the military's public voice on Chinese pressure, including the December 2025 radar lock-on incident, and opened an official X account in July 2026.

December 2025 radar lock-on incident: he rejected China's account, saying ASDF fighters, on this and every occasion, comply with international and domestic law and keep a safe distance while carrying out their mission.

July 2026: opened an official X account to explain joint operations and SDF activity, amid what Japan calls Chinese cognitive warfare. He said he would coordinate posts with those concerned rather than post freely.

Trilateral Chiefs of Defense meeting, Washington, 15 Jul 2026: agreed with the US and ROK chiefs to deepen multi-domain cooperation against North Korea's nuclear and missile threat, to keep up the annual FREEDOM EDGE exercise, and for Japan to host the 2027 meeting.

His five priorities on taking office (1 Aug 2025) are the 'five I's': Integration, Interoperability, Inter-connectivity, Intensity and Innovation. He was still answering questions on them at his 3 Apr 2026 press conference. This replaces the partial list in part B.
Video call with India's Chief of Defence Staff, Gen. N. S. Raja Subramani, 16 Sep 2026: the two agreed to deepen Japan–India defence cooperation.

interests.text: Says he has carried Saigo Takamori's collected teachings (Nanshu-o Ikun) since childhood and rereads them at career milestones; gives 'shisei' (utmost sincerity) as his motto (first press conference as Chief of Staff, 4 Aug 2025, as reported by Asagumo).

hooks.text: He made his introductory visit to Singapore on 10–12 Aug 2026, calling on Minister Chan Chun Sing and CDF VADM Aaron Beng and visiting Paya Lebar Air Base for a brief on RSAF Smart Airbase work. The follow-up writes itself: airbase resilience and integrated air and missile defence, which he names as urgent.

He uses multilateral chiefs' meetings for bilateral contact. At SLD 2026 he met counterparts including Singapore's, and at the August 2025 Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defense conference he held 13 bilaterals, Singapore among them. SLD and the CHOD conference are the realistic CDF-level touchpoints.
A fighter pilot, former Air Defense Command commander and two-time Air University student, he shares a common air-power and US-PME frame with RSAF leadership.
Rapport openers: his Kagoshima roots, Saigo Takamori's teachings and his motto of sincerity, all of which he raised himself in his first press conference.

He uses multilateral meetings to reach beyond the region. At SLD 2026 he met the Chair of the NATO Military Committee, Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, and in Sep 2026 he held a video call with India's CDS. A CDF-level video call between SLD meetings fits his pattern.

bio.text: Career GSDF officer who was Commanding General of the Western Army until July 2025, when he was named the 40th Chief of Staff, GSDF from 1 Aug 2025. In office he has pressed stand-off missile deployments, unit reorganisation, unmanned systems and counter-drone training. He led the GSDF through the April 2026 accident at Hijudai, where a round burst during Type 10 tank firing and killed three soldiers. He made his introductory visit to Singapore in September 2025, and in September 2026 became the first GSDF chief to visit South Korea in 17 years.

positions.text: New Year message, 1 Jan 2026: set 'creating a robust GSDF' as his theme.
Press conference, 24 Feb 2026: the GSDF held about 1,200 unmanned assets at the end of FY2024. He discussed small attack drones and lessons from the war in Ukraine.
Said the GSDF–Indian Army exercise Dharma Guardian (Feb–Mar 2026) would include counter-drone training.

Stand-off and anti-ship missiles: briefed new and reorganised units and stand-off missile deployment (Mar 2026), preparation of surface-to-ship missile units on Minamitorishima (Jun 2026) and a Type 88 surface-to-ship missile live-fire at Shizunai, Hokkaido (Aug 2026). He said the GSDF would keep raising unit proficiency.
After the Hijudai accident (21 Apr 2026) he apologised, set up an investigation committee at Western Army HQ and suspended Type 10 main-gun firing and Type 90 firing with the same ammunition.

Press conference, 17 Mar 2026: announced an Information Operations Unit under the Ground Component Command from 23 Mar 2026. Other states, he said, already use disinformation and strategic messaging before any conflict to sway public opinion and decision-making. Units had been analysing disinformation and protecting decision-making separately, so the GSDF needed one coherent structure for information warfare.
Press conference, 4 Aug 2026: surface-to-ship missile regiments will train this fiscal year in command-and-staff work coordinated with electronic-warfare units.

hooks.text: He already knows Singapore: on his September 2025 introductory visit he met SMS Zaqy Mohamad and senior SAF officers, and both sides reaffirmed warm defence ties. A Chief of Army return contact builds on an existing relationship.

Unmanned systems and counter-drone training are a stated focus (about 1,200 UAS, Ukraine lessons, counter-drone work with India). This matches the SAF's own counter-UAS learning agenda and could support an army-to-army exchange.

He is opening new army-to-army channels: talks with the French Army chief (Feb 2026) and the first GSDF chief's visit to Korea in 17 years (Sep 2026). That suggests he would welcome a proposal for Singapore Army–GSDF staff talks.

Island logistics is a live GSDF topic: a new small transport vessel built for small ports and islands was due to be named and launched on 17 Sep 2026. This fits SAF interest in littoral manoeuvre and sustainment.

He uses army chiefs' conferences for bilaterals. He met ROK Army chief Gen. Kim Gyu-ha at LANPAC in Hawaii (May 2026), then visited Seoul on 29–30 Sep 2026, the first visit by a GSDF chief in 17 years, to discuss North Korea and defence cooperation. LANPAC is a realistic venue for a Singapore Army chief bilateral.

He is an armour and reconnaissance officer (1st Tank Group, 10th Reconnaissance Unit, 2nd Tank Regiment) who has also done joint operations planning (Joint Staff J3), and he was Vice President of the National Defense Academy (2023–24). Armour modernisation, joint planning and officer education are natural professional openers.

As a US-alliance specialist (former Director-General, North American Affairs) and Tokyo's channel to the US national security adviser, he is the best-placed source on where Tokyo and Washington align on the region.

scholarship.title: The proposed hike in Japan's military expenditure (Topical Backgrounder)
scholarship.takeaway: The FY2023 SDF budget of ¥6.8 trillion (~$52bn) was 26% above 2022, the largest year-on-year nominal rise in planned military spending since at least 1952. The 2022 NSS targets 2% of GDP for 'defence and other outlays' by 2027.

scholarship.title: Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2025 (Fact Sheet)
scholarship.takeaway: Japan spent $62.2bn in 2025 (+9.7%, 61% above 2016), or 1.4% of GDP, its highest burden since 1958. SIPRI ties the rise to the 2022 build-up plan and to concern over China and North Korea.

scholarship.title: Japan's military recruitment crisis in an age of rearmament

scholarship.title: Japan's Official Security Assistance to Southeast Asia: Limited Scope, but Real Impact
scholarship.author: John Bradford; Raymond Yamamoto
scholarship.takeaway: OSA started small (about ¥2bn in year one, with coastal radars for the Philippines and rescue boats for Malaysia) but already shapes military cooperation in Southeast Asia. It is Japan's new tool for building partner forces in the region.

scholarship.title: Japan's 'three national security documents' and defense capabilities: reinforcing a radical military trajectory
scholarship.author: Christopher W. Hughes
scholarship.takeaway: Argues that the 2022 documents continue and harden a long-running, radical turn in Japan's military posture rather than marking a sudden break. Only the title and listing were captured.

scholarship.title: Not Always Easy: Lessons Learned on Introducing New Defense Capabilities in Japan
scholarship.author: Jeffrey W. Hornung and others (full author list not captured)
scholarship.takeaway: Ten case studies of introducing new US and Japanese capabilities and bases in Japan. Planners cannot assume that deployment requests will go smoothly, which bears on the pace of counterstrike and island deployments.

scholarship.title: Beyond Policy Limits: Rethinking U.S.-Japan Command and Control
scholarship.author: Stimson Center Japan Program, 'Views from the Next Generation' series (byline not confirmed)
scholarship.takeaway: The planned upgrades (Japan's Joint Operations Command, and US Forces Japan becoming a joint force HQ under INDOPACOM) look like progress, but existing policy and structures still limit them.

scholarship.title: Japan's Grand Strategy: Liminal Power in an Uncertain World
scholarship.author: Saori Katada; Kei Koga
scholarship.takeaway: Treats Japan's Indo-Pacific strategy as a long process of institutional adaptation, not only a reaction to China, with the East China Sea as a test case. It is co-written by an NTU (Singapore) scholar.

why.text: Japan runs the region's largest military disaster responses. After the 2011 earthquake the SDF deployed up to about 107,000 personnel, 540 aircraft and 59 ships, under its first joint task force for disaster relief. For the January 2024 Noto earthquake a joint ground, maritime and air team peaked at up to 14,000, and about 10,000 mostly Ground SDF personnel stayed on for months of daily-life support.

learn_from.what: How Japan stands up a joint task force for a domestic catastrophe, hands over from rescue to sustained life support (water, bathing, supplies) and scales down, and how it would take in foreign military help, which Changi RHCC is built to coordinate.

learn_from.domain: Manpower under a shrinking youth population

why.text: The SDF met only 51% of its FY2023 recruiting target (9,959 of 19,598) and was running at about 90% of its ~247,000 authorised strength in 2024. MOD expects the recruitable cohort to keep shrinking. A December 2024 package added more than 30 new allowances, and recruitment reportedly rose to 11,177 in FY2025. MOD is extending re-employment support to age 65, and analysts urge building the force around labour-saving and unmanned capabilities. The SAF faces the same trend: average annual full-time NS enlistment to the SAF fell from 19,100 (2016–20) to 17,300 (2021–25).

learn_from.what: Evidence on which pay, allowance, re-employment (to age 65) and career measures actually moved recruiting and retention, and how MOD plans around fewer people with labour-saving steps: AI base surveillance expected to free about 1,000 personnel, automated storage, and lean crews such as the ~90-person Mogami-class frigate.

why.text: Japan's FY2026 budget puts ¥100.1bn into SHIELD, a layered coastal defence built from several thousand aerial, surface and underwater drones of about 10 types. It will rely mainly on imported, off-the-shelf systems at first and is due by the end of FY2027 (one report says March 2028). Few militaries in the region are fielding unmanned systems this fast.

learn_from.what: How Japan specifies, buys, integrates and trains for thousands of low-cost drones in two years, how it balances imports against domestic industry, and how unmanned layers tie into manned coastal defence. This bears on the SAF's DARE and counter-UAS work and on the unmanned-systems exchanges the 2026 Strategic Partnership names.

why.text: Japan stood up the Joint Operations Command on 24 Mar 2025 with about 240 staff (planned to grow to 280) to command the Ground, Maritime and Air SDF in peacetime and in conflict. Its stated priorities are seamless response to incidents, cross-domain operations and cooperation with partners. Its second commander, Adm. Tawara, took over in March 2026, and Australia has reportedly posted a liaison officer to it.

learn_from.what: Design choices for a permanent joint operational headquarters: span of command, staffing and growth, how allies and partners are linked in through liaison officers, and how a new headquarters is exercised in its first years.

why.text: Japan's 2023 Act on Enhancing Defense Production and Technology Bases lets MOD survey supply-chain risks, fund suppliers directly, take over production facilities and raise contractor margins to up to 15%. Certified company plans grew from 36 in FY2023 to 121 in FY2024. In April 2026 the government scrapped the five non-combat export categories, so lethal equipment can now go case by case to the 17 countries with transfer agreements. Australia chose the upgraded Mogami-class frigate in August 2025.

learn_from.what: Supply-chain risk-mapping methods and government-to-government co-development models, and what Japan's new rules could mean for the 2023 Japan–Singapore transfer agreement in technology, sustainment and supply-chain resilience. The aim is method, not a shopping list.

relationship.text: Warm, steady and widening, but still built mostly on dialogue, visits, port calls and multilateral exercises rather than deep operational ties. The machinery is solid: policy talks since 1997, a defence-exchange memorandum from 2009 (enhanced in 2022) and a 2023 equipment-transfer agreement. 2026 added a Strategic Partnership, a regular defence ministers' meeting at the Shangri-La Dialogue and the first branded bilateral naval exercise, Singapan. No equipment transfer, standing training arrangement, or bilateral army or air exercise has been made public, and no SAF training detachment in Japan has been reported.

engagement.angle: Use the 60th-anniversary Strategic Partnership and Singapore's role as ASEAN–Japan coordinator (to 2027) to turn goodwill into a few working-level exchanges on problems both forces share: fewer young people, lean-manned and unmanned forces, and large-scale disaster response. Treat Japan as a learn-from partner on scale and method, and offer Singapore's coordination platforms (Changi RHCC, IFC) and NS experience in return.
we_want: Lessons from Japan's manpower squeeze: which pay, allowance, re-employment and labour-saving measures actually moved recruiting and retention
Practical know-how on fielding unmanned systems at scale (SHIELD) and on lean-manned ship design (Mogami-class, ~90 crew)
JJOC's experience standing up a permanent joint operational command, including how it links in partners
Japan's playbook for very large domestic disasters: joint task force stand-up and the shift from rescue to months of life support
Insight into Japan's defence-industrial base and post-April 2026 export rules, and what the 2023 transfer agreement could support for supply-chain resilience
we_offer: Changi RHCC's multinational coordination tools (OPERA CIS 2.0) and MNCC experience, already used alongside the JSDF at RIMPAC 2026
Singapore's experience running National Service, reservists and volunteers (SAFVC) with a shrinking cohort, including drone training for every service-fit recruit
RSN experience operating autonomous MARSEC USVs with two-person crews in the congested Singapore Strait
Singapore's convening role as ASEAN–Japan coordinator to 2027 and incoming ASEAN chair, plus the Shangri-La Dialogue platform
Changi Naval Base for JMSDF deployments, IFC maritime information-sharing and Pacific Reach submarine-rescue cooperation

sg_ties.text: Singapore and Japan established diplomatic relations on 26 April 1966. Prime Ministers Wong and Takaichi exchanged letters for the 60th anniversary on 26 April 2026.

Defence Ministers Teo Chee Hean and Kitazawa Toshimi signed the Memorandum on Defence Exchanges in December 2009. It formalised visits by defence officials, policy dialogues, military staff talks and cross-attendance of courses and seminars, and opened cooperation on HADR and peace support operations.

Ministers Ng Eng Hen and Kishi Nobuo signed an Enhanced Memorandum on Defence Exchanges at the Shangri-La Dialogue. It added logistics support, defence-technology exchanges, CBRE protection, strategic communications and maritime security, and the two sides launched talks on an equipment-transfer agreement.

The Agreement concerning the Transfer of Defense Equipment and Technology was signed at the Shangri-La Dialogue by Permanent Secretary (Defence Development) Melvyn Ong and Ambassador Ishikawa Hiroshi, and entered into force the same day. It sets controls on re-transfer to third parties but does not oblige either side to buy or sell. MINDEF says it gives the SAF more options for training and operational needs.

At the Shangri-La Dialogue, Ministers Nakatani Gen and Chan Chun Sing discussed cyber exchanges and defence-technology research. Japan's readout notes that Singapore is ASEAN's coordinator country for Japan from 2024 to 2027, a role Singapore's leaders also cited in August 2025 and February 2026.

A SAFTI Military Institute delegation made its first visit to Japan's Joint Staff College. Japan's National Defense Academy lists Singapore among the countries sending foreign cadets and runs short exchange visits with Singapore's academy. MINDEF regularly cites cross-attendance of courses, but gives no numbers.

Japan sent the submarine JS Kuroshio and the rescue ship JS Chiyoda to Exercise Pacific Reach 2025, hosted by the RSN at Changi (17 countries, about 600 participants). JMSDF ships also called at Changi in 2023 (the IMED23 unit, and JS Kumano for IMDEX Asia) and joined IMDEX Asia 2025.

The 20th JMOD–MINDEF Policy Talks were held in Tokyo, led by Director General of the Bureau of Defense Policy Arima Takanori and Deputy Secretary (Policy) BG Frederick Choo. They covered regional affairs and the future direction of cooperation. The talks, earlier called the Military-to-Military Dialogue, have been held periodically since 1997.

Prime Ministers Lawrence Wong and Takaichi Sanae upgraded relations to a Strategic Partnership. Its security pillar commits to a regular defence ministers' meeting at the Shangri-La Dialogue, closer collaboration between operational authorities through bilateral and multilateral exercises, exchanges on common platforms, lean-manning concepts and unmanned systems, and further equipment and technology cooperation under the 2023 agreement.

Ministers Koizumi Shinjirō and Chan Chun Sing met at the Shangri-La Dialogue, after an earlier meeting at the ADMM-Plus in Kuala Lumpur on 1 Nov 2025. They agreed to meet regularly, to work through working groups of the JMOD–MINDEF Policy Talks, to continue high-level visits and unit-level engagements such as port calls, and to advance equipment and technology cooperation within existing legal frameworks.

At RIMPAC 2026, RSS Steadfast sailed in a JMSDF-led Multinational Group Sail from Guam to Hawaii, and Changi RHCC worked with JSDF personnel on its OPERA CIS 2.0 system in the HADR exercise. In 2024 an RSN-led group sail to RIMPAC included the JMSDF's JS Kunisaki.

Senior military visits now run both ways. Chief of Staff, Joint Staff Gen. Uchikura Hiroaki made an introductory visit (10–12 Aug 2026), calling on Minister Chan and CDF VADM Aaron Beng and seeing RSAF Smart Airbase and counter-UAS capabilities. Before him came the JGSDF Chief of Staff (Sep 2025, briefed on the SAF's Centre of Excellence for Soldier Performance), the JASDF Vice Chief of Staff (Singapore Airshow, Feb 2026), and Chief of Army MG David Neo's official visit to Japan (Oct 2024).

The RSN and JMSDF held Exercise Singapan off Japan on 27–28 Aug 2026, with RSS Steadfast alongside JS Hamagiri and JS Teruzuki. It covered sea-rider exchanges, gunnery, communications and manoeuvring, and a JMSDF helicopter cross-deck. Janes calls it the inaugural edition. RSS Steadfast hosted Navy@Tokyo on 21–22 Aug. Earlier bilateral drills, such as a 2018 passage exercise off Yokosuka, were not branded.

Japan is expanding Official Security Assistance in the region: about ¥18.1bn in FY2026 for 10–12 countries, including the Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia, moving from components to complete systems. Singapore is not a recipient and appears in no list seen; for Singapore the relevant channel is the 2023 transfer agreement, not OSA.

venues.name: National Defense Academy of Japan (NDA), Yokosuka
venues.note: Japan's officer academy. It has about 100 foreign cadets from 11 countries, Singapore among them; most study Japanese for a year and then take the full four-year degree. NDA cadets make one- to three-week visits to partner academies, including Singapore's, and Singaporean cadets visit the NDA for ten-day stays.

venues.name: Joint Staff College (JSC), Tokyo
venues.note: Japan's joint staff college. A SAFTI MI delegation made its first visit in Sep 2025. JSC notices say international student officers attend by mutual agreement between Japan and the home country, and past courses have included foreign officers (10 of 192 in an FY2014 course, and an ROK officer in a Joint Advanced Course). No Singaporean attendance was found.

venues.name: JMSDF Command and Staff College, Tokyo
venues.note: Educates senior JMSDF officers for command and staff posts. In 2016, with the US Naval War College, it began an Asia-Pacific Navy Planning Process International Course that trains regional naval staff officers to plan HADR operations. Whether the course still runs, and who can attend, is not confirmed.

venues.name: Japan–ASEAN Professional Airmanship Programme and Ship Rider Cooperation (Vientiane Vision)
venues.note: Japan-run programmes for ASEAN officers. The JASDF invites ASEAN air officers to Japan (announced 2018), and the Ship Rider Cooperation embarks ASEAN officers on JMSDF ships. Both now sit under Japan's JASMINE initiative (2023). Current editions and Singapore's participation were not checked.

venues.name: Exercise Singapan (RSN–JMSDF)
venues.note: Bilateral naval exercise. The first edition (27–28 Aug 2026, off Japan) paired RSS Steadfast with JS Hamagiri and JS Teruzuki. No future cycle has been announced.

venues.name: Exercise Pacific Reach (submarine escape and rescue)
venues.note: Multinational submarine escape and rescue exercise. The RSN hosted the ninth and largest edition (15–29 Sep 2025, 17 countries), with Japan contributing JS Kuroshio and the rescue ship JS Chiyoda.

venues.name: RIMPAC and Multinational Group Sails
venues.note: Biennial US-hosted maritime exercise. In 2026 RSS Steadfast sailed in a JMSDF-led group sail from Guam to Hawaii, and Changi RHCC worked with JSDF personnel in the HADR exercise. In 2024 the RSN led a group sail that included a JMSDF ship.

venues.name: ADMM-Plus Experts' Working Group on Maritime Security (Japan–Philippines co-chairs, 2024–2027)
venues.note: Japan and the Philippines co-hosted a Joint Cooperative Activity off Subic Bay (21–25 Sep 2026) for ADMM-Plus navies, with SME exchanges on confidence-building, search and rescue, casualty evacuation and maritime security drills. RSS Justice took part. A way to work with Japan inside an ASEAN-led format.

venues.name: Exercise Pitch Black (Australia)
venues.note: Biennial RAAF-hosted air combat exercise. The 2026 edition (Darwin, 20 Jul–7 Aug) had 21 nations including Japan and Singapore; the RSAF sent eight F-16s, a G550 AEW aircraft and over 200 personnel. The RSAF has also trained with the JASDF at Red Flag-Alaska.

venues.name: Exercise Super Garuda Shield (Indonesia)
venues.note: Multinational exercise co-hosted by Indonesia and the US. The 2026 edition (31 Aug–11 Sep) had 14 armed forces including Japan and Singapore, with joint staff planning, cyber defence and civic action. DIS took part in the cyber defence exercise.

venues.name: JMSDF International Fleet Review and Western Pacific Naval Symposium
venues.note: RSS Formidable joined the 2022 Fleet Review for the JMSDF's 70th anniversary (38 ships from 13 countries) and a JMSDF-led multilateral search-and-rescue exercise. Singapore's Chief of Navy attended the WPNS held alongside. The next review date was not found.

venues.name: Shangri-La Dialogue, Singapore (Japan–Singapore defence ministers' meeting)
venues.note: The 2026 Strategic Partnership commits to a regular defence ministers' meeting at the SLD; the ministers met there in 2025 and 2026. The SLD has also been used for signings (the 2022 enhanced memorandum and the 2023 transfer agreement).

venues.name: Japan–ASEAN Defense Vice-Ministerial Forum and ASEAN–Japan Defence Ministers' Informal Meeting
venues.note: Japan's main defence forums with ASEAN. The 14th Vice-Ministerial Forum (Feb 2025) reviewed progress under JASMINE, which Japan launched at the ministers' meeting in Nov 2023. Singapore co-chaired the ministers' meeting in 2018 and, as coordinator to 2027, has a convening role.

venues.name: Singapore Airshow and IMDEX Asia (Singapore)
venues.note: Japan sends senior officers and ships to Singapore's defence shows. The JASDF Vice Chief of Staff attended the Singapore Airshow and the first Space Summit in Feb 2026, and JMSDF ships joined IMDEX Asia in 2023 and 2025. These are low-cost meeting points.

saf_units.name: Defence Policy Group (DPG)
saf_units.role: Handles MINDEF's relations with its foreign counterparts, strategic communications, National Education, Total Defence, strategic planning and futures analysis, and inter-ministry coordination on emerging security threats.

saf_units.name: Defence Policy Office (DPO)
saf_units.role: Develops strategy and directs efforts to strengthen bilateral defence relations with partner countries, build an open and inclusive regional security architecture, and contribute to international security. Its Deputy Secretary (Policy) leads Singapore's side of the JMOD–MINDEF Policy Talks.

saf_units.name: SAFTI Military Institute (SAFTI MI)
saf_units.role: Tri-service, tri-level institute of the SAF and home of the SAF Officer Corps. It includes the Goh Keng Swee Command and Staff College, SAF Advanced Schools, Officer Cadet School and Specialist and Warrant Officer Institute. A SAFTI MI delegation made its first visit to Japan's Joint Staff College in Sep 2025.

saf_units.name: Goh Keng Swee Command and Staff College (GKS CSC)
saf_units.role: Prepares officers for senior command and staff appointments. It is the highest level of formal military education in Singapore for Regular, NS and International Officers, and graduated 23 international officers from 12 countries in 2025. It hosts a Distinguished Leaders Dialogue, which Lithuania's CHOD addressed in 2026.

saf_units.name: SAF Joint Staff
saf_units.role: The SAF's joint staff, led by the Chief of Staff–Joint Staff, who joined the civil-military coordination discussions at Exercise COORES 2025. The sources found here do not describe its functions in detail.

saf_units.name: Changi Regional HADR Coordination Centre (Changi RHCC)
saf_units.role: SAF centre that helps militaries coordinate multinational disaster response. It runs OPERA CIS 2.0, a web platform for military-military and civil-military coordination through Multinational Coordination Centre processes, and co-organises Exercise COORES. In April 2016 Singapore offered an RHCC team to help the JSDF coordinate foreign military assistance after earthquakes in Japan.

saf_units.name: RSN Fleet (incl. submarine rescue)
saf_units.role: The RSN's Fleet Commander directed Exercise Pacific Reach 2025, which the RSN hosted. Its submarine rescue capability is the support and rescue vessel MV Swift Rescue with the DSAR 6 rescue vehicle.

saf_units.name: First Flotilla, RSN
saf_units.role: Frigate flotilla. Its commander co-officiated Exercise Singapan 2026 with the JMSDF at Yokosuka and led the RSN task group (RSS Steadfast) at RIMPAC 2026.

saf_units.name: Information Fusion Centre (IFC)
saf_units.role: Maritime information-sharing centre with International Liaison Officers attached. Its IRIS 2.0 web system was used at sea for the first time at the 2nd ASEAN–India Maritime Exercise (2026).

saf_units.name: Centre of Excellence for Soldier Performance (CESP)
saf_units.role: Develops equipment and systems to optimise soldier performance, including heat-strain monitoring, pre-habilitation exercises, training curriculum design and an integrated soldier system. It briefed the JGSDF Chief of Staff in Sep 2025.

saf_units.name: SAF Volunteer Corps (SAFVC)
saf_units.role: Volunteer corps founded in 2015. About 1,500 volunteers from diverse backgrounds have served in its first ten years, supporting SAF operations and training.

saf_units.name: Central Manpower Base (CMPB)
saf_units.role: Handles National Service registration, pre-enlistment medical examination and deferment applications under the Enlistment Act.

saf_units.name: Nexus
saf_units.role: The lead agency in MINDEF/SAF that drives National Education and Total Defence. Total Defence has six pillars: military, civil, economic, social, digital and psychological.

saf_units.name: Digital and Intelligence Service (DIS)
saf_units.role: The SAF's fourth service, inaugurated in October 2022. It raises, trains and sustains digital forces and capabilities, with a mission to 'defend and dominate in the digital domain' across intelligence, C4 and cyber. DIS took part in the cyber defence exercise at Super Garuda Shield 2026, alongside Japan.

saf_units.name: Defence Cyber Command
saf_units.role: DIS command inaugurated in March 2025 from the Cybersecurity Task Force and Defence Cyber Organisation. It defends MINDEF/SAF against cyber threats and partners Whole-of-Government to support national cyber defence.

saf_units.name: SAF Counter-UAS Development and Operations Group
saf_units.short: SAF Counter-UAS Development and Operations Group
saf_units.role: Announced by the Minister for Defence on 2025-03-03, to be formed with other government agencies. It targets the small-drone threat, adding sensors, jammers and weapons to existing air defence. Its stand-up date is not confirmed in sources found.

saf_units.name: Drone Accelerator for Rapid Equipping (DARE), Singapore Army
saf_units.role: Army initiative announced in 2025 to quickly equip the force with UAS and scale up UAV and unmanned ground vehicle operations. Exact status is not confirmed. Separately, the SAF plans to train all service-fit recruits to operate and counter drones.

saf_units.name: RSAF UAS Warfare and Tactics Centre
saf_units.short: RSAF UAS Warfare and Tactics Centre
saf_units.role: Leads efforts to develop counter-UAS strategies and integrate them with the broader SAF. Announced in 2025.

saf_units.name: Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA)
saf_units.role: MINDEF statutory board, formed in 2000, that performs acquisitions management, systems management and systems development for MINDEF and the SAF across the system life cycle. It co-developed the RSN's autonomous MARSEC USVs with DSO.

saf_units.name: DSO National Laboratories
saf_units.role: Defence R&D organisation in MINDEF's Defence Technology Community, described as Singapore's largest defence R&D organisation. It researches emerging technologies and develops defence systems for the SAF.

saf_units.name: Future Systems and Technology Directorate (FSTD)
saf_units.role: Plans and manages MINDEF/SAF research and technology needs. It is the master-planning office for concepts and systems development and includes the SAF Centre for Military Experimentation.

saf_units.name: Defence Technology Collaboration Office (DTCO)
saf_units.role: Leads strategy for international and local defence technology collaboration, builds strategic partnerships with foreign governments and hosts high-level dialogues. It reports to Deputy Secretary (Technology).

lines.name: Policy channel under the Strategic Partnership
lines.objective: Use the new regular SLD ministers' meeting and the Policy Talks working groups to agree a short, named work plan (manpower and lean-manning, unmanned systems, HADR, defence technology) that sponsors the other lines.

basis.text: The machinery exists. The 2026 Strategic Partnership commits to a regular ministers' meeting at the SLD, the May 2026 meeting agreed to work through Policy Talks working groups, and the talks reached their 20th round in March 2026. What is missing is a published agenda of practical projects.

activities.text: At SLD 2027, have the Ministers endorse a two-year work plan drawn from the Strategic Partnership's named areas: exercises, common platforms, lean-manning and unmanned systems.
Stand up two Policy Talks working groups first, on (a) manpower and lean-manning and (b) defence technology and supply-chain resilience, and have both report at the 21st round.

Use Singapore's ASEAN–Japan coordinator role (to 2027) and its 2027 ASEAN chairmanship to line bilateral projects up with Japan's JASMINE agenda in the ADMM-Plus, and invite Japan to consider joining the GUIDE framework on undersea infrastructure.
Start the cyber exchanges the ministers discussed in May 2025, between DIS Defence Cyber Command and JSDF cyber counterparts.

counterparts: Minister of Defense (Koizumi Shinjirō was the SLD interlocutor in 2025–26)
MOD Bureau of Defense Policy (Director General Arima Takanori led the 2026 Policy Talks)
MOD Director General for International Affairs (led earlier rounds of the Military-to-Military Dialogue)
we_offer: Convening power as ASEAN–Japan coordinator to 2027 and 2027 ASEAN chair
The Shangri-La Dialogue as a regular meeting point
A small, fast partner for testing practical ideas before Japan scales them to ASEAN

lines.name: Navy to navy: Singapan, submarine rescue and maritime security
lines.objective: Make Exercise Singapan a regular series, and extend RSN–JMSDF cooperation into submarine rescue, unmanned maritime systems and maritime domain awareness.

basis.text: This is the most mature line. The two navies held their first branded bilateral exercise in Aug 2026, meet in group sails and at RIMPAC, and Japan brought a submarine and a rescue ship to Pacific Reach 2025 at Changi. JMSDF deployments already call at Changi.

activities.text: Agree a cycle for Exercise Singapan, alternating between waters off Japan and Singapore during JMSDF Indo-Pacific Deployments that call at Changi.
Add a bilateral submarine escape and rescue serial (MV Swift Rescue/DSAR 6 with a JMSDF rescue ship) building on Pacific Reach 2025.
Show JMSDF officers MARSEC USV operations and the IFC's IRIS 2.0 system, and ask whether Japan will post an International Liaison Officer to the IFC (not confirmed in sources).
Keep port calls and public events such as Navy@Tokyo (Aug 2026) as goodwill anchors.

counterparts: Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (Surface Warfare Squadron Nine co-officiated Singapan 2026)
JMSDF submarine rescue units (JS Chiyoda at Pacific Reach 2025)
we_offer: Changi Naval Base for JMSDF deployment port calls
IFC maritime information-sharing (IRIS 2.0)
Submarine rescue capability (MV Swift Rescue with DSAR 6)
Autonomous USV operating experience in congested waters

lines.name: HADR and large-scale disaster response
lines.objective: Build a bilateral HADR channel between Changi RHCC and the JSDF, so the SAF learns how Japan runs very large domestic disaster responses and Japan knows how to use RHCC tools in a regional crisis.

basis.text: Japan has run the region's largest military disaster responses (up to about 107,000 SDF personnel in 2011, and a joint team of up to 14,000 for Noto in 2024). Changi RHCC and JSDF personnel already used OPERA CIS 2.0 together at RIMPAC 2026, and Singapore offered an RHCC team to Japan after the April 2016 earthquakes. The two also co-chaired the ADMM-Plus Experts' Working Group on Military Medicine in its first cycle (to 2013), which produced HADR medical SOPs. Bilateral HADR work so far has happened only inside multilateral events.

activities.text: RHCC–JSDF SME exchange on Multinational Coordination Centre procedures and OPERA CIS 2.0.
Invite JSDF planners to the next Exercise COORES (biennial; 39 militaries and 37 civil organisations took part in 2025) and to RHCC's Humanitarian Futures Forum.
Ask for observer places at a JSDF large-scale disaster-response exercise or a JJOC partner HADR rehearsal.
Jointly study the Noto 2024 shift from rescue to sustained life support, to inform SAF homeland HADR planning.

counterparts: Japan Joint Staff (Chief of Staff Gen. Uchikura Hiroaki visited Singapore in Aug 2026)
Japan Ground Self-Defense Force (main source of disaster-relief manpower)
we_offer: OPERA CIS 2.0 and MNCC processes
Exercise COORES as a ready-made venue
RHCC's regional HADR network through the ADMM-Plus

lines.name: Manpower, lean-manning and unmanned systems
lines.objective: Run a structured exchange on doing more with fewer people: recruitment and retention as the youth cohort shrinks, lean-manned platforms, and fielding unmanned systems at scale.

basis.text: Both forces have shrinking intakes. Average annual SAF NS enlistment fell from 19,100 (2016–20) to 17,300 (2021–25), and the SDF met 51% of its FY2023 recruiting target. The 2026 Strategic Partnership names lean-manning and unmanned systems as exchange areas, and Japan's SHIELD programme (¥100.1bn in FY2026 for several thousand drones) is a large live experiment.

activities.text: Manpower staff talks between MINDEF manpower and NS policy staff and the MOD Bureau of Personnel and Education, on what Japan's December 2024 pay and allowance package and re-employment to age 65 did for recruiting and retention.
RSN–JMSDF exchange on lean-manned ship design and crewing (Mogami-class, ~90 crew) and on two-person-crewed MARSEC USVs.
Army and RSAF SME exchange on drone and counter-drone training. The SAF is training all service-fit recruits to operate and counter drones, and Japan is fielding SHIELD.
Follow up the JGSDF and Joint Staff chiefs' visits to CESP and RSAF Smart Airbase with an SAF visit to a SHIELD unit once fielded.

counterparts: MOD Bureau of Personnel and Education
Japan Ground Self-Defense Force Staff Office (its Chief of Staff visited Singapore in Sep 2025)
we_offer: Decades of NS and reservist management with a shrinking cohort
Drone training for every service-fit recruit, and NS units using drones in in-camp training from mid-2026
MARSEC USV autonomy and verification experience (over 1,000 hours of autonomous operations)
The SAFVC volunteer model (about 1,500 volunteers in ten years)

lines.name: Defence technology and supply-chain resilience
lines.objective: Put the 2023 transfer agreement to its first practical use, through technology exchanges and a supply-chain resilience arrangement, without implying any purchase.

basis.text: The 2023 agreement gives a legal framework, but no project has been announced. Ministers discussed defence-technology research in 2025 and in 2026 agreed to advance cooperation 'within existing legal frameworks'. Since then Singapore has signed supply-chain arrangements with Germany (Mar 2026), Italy (May 2026) and Australia (Jul 2026), and Japan's April 2026 rule change widens what Japan can transfer.

activities.text: DTCO talks with Japan's Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency to map candidate areas such as autonomy, unmanned systems and protective technologies.
Explore a Japan–Singapore supply-chain resilience arrangement modelled on those signed with Germany, Italy and Australia.
Exchanges between DSO and Japanese defence research bodies on autonomy and sensing, under the 2023 agreement's transfer controls.

counterparts: Ministry of Defense (equipment and technology cooperation under the 2023 agreement)
Embassy of Japan in Singapore (signatory of the 2023 agreement)
we_offer: DSTA and DSO autonomy and systems-integration experience (e.g. MARSEC USV)
A tested template for supply-chain resilience arrangements
Singapore as a regional maintenance and logistics node (e.g. the 2026 TKMS–ST Engineering submarine maintenance MOU)

lines.name: Professional military education and joint command
lines.objective: Deepen course cross-attendance beyond cadet level and learn from JJOC's first years as a standing joint headquarters.

basis.text: Course cross-attendance is long-standing, Singapore sends cadets to Japan's NDA, and SAFTI MI made its first visit to Japan's Joint Staff College in Sep 2025. JJOC, stood up in March 2025, is the SDF's biggest command reform and lists cooperation with partners as a priority; Australia has reportedly posted a liaison officer to it.

activities.text: Seek a place for an SAF officer on the JSC Joint Advanced Course (JSC takes international students by mutual agreement), and offer a GKS CSC place to a JSDF officer.
Host a return visit by Japan's Joint Staff College to SAFTI MI, and invite a senior JSDF leader to the GKS CSC Distinguished Leaders Dialogue.
Joint Staff talks with JJOC on standing joint HQ design, partner liaison and cross-domain operations.
Ask for observer status at a JJOC-run exercise with partners, for example HADR or cross-domain serials.

counterparts: Japan Joint Operations Command (Commander Adm. Tawara since March 2026)
we_offer: GKS CSC places (23 international officers from 12 countries graduated in 2025)
SAFTI MI's tri-service, tri-level education model
Integrated SAF joint operations experience

precedents.text: Exercise Panzer Strike: the SAF has trained armour in Germany since 2009, at Oberlausitz since 2016. The 17th edition (28 Feb–19 Mar 2026) had about 80 personnel from 48 SAR with Leopard 2SG and Hunter AFVs alongside 130+ from Panzergrenadierbataillon 391. It is a model of steady bilateral training in a partner's space, with professional exchanges built in.

During Defence Minister Pistorius's March 2026 visit, Singapore and Germany signed a Supply Chain Resiliency Arrangement and witnessed a TKMS–ST Engineering Marine MOU on submarine maintenance; Pistorius was also briefed on National Service. In Oct 2026 the ministers agreed to work on cybersecurity, hybrid threats, defence industry and supply chains. It is a model of an industrial partner relationship anchored in a defence cooperation agreement (enhanced 2018).

Singapore and Italy concluded an MoU on Supply Chain Resiliency on the sidelines of the 2026 Shangri-La Dialogue, signed by MINDEF's Permanent Secretary (Defence Development) and Italy's National Armaments Director. This shows how SLD sideline meetings can deliver a practical agreement with a non-ally.

The Australia–Singapore MOU concerning Enhanced Defence Cooperation (Oct 2025) covers reciprocal access, more SAF training in Australia, a planned RSAF Rotational Fighter Training Detachment, defence science and technology, and logistics and supply chains. It was followed by an Industrial Base Resiliency Arrangement in July 2026. This is the most complete SAF partnership package.

Since 1998 the RSAF has kept its Advanced Jet Training Detachment (150 Squadron, M-346) at Cazaux Air Base. In 27 years it has flown over 31,000 hours and trained more than 330 fighter pilots and weapon systems officers. It is the highest form of SAF presence with a European partner.

Exercise Bold Kurukshetra, a bilateral armour exercise first held in 2005, runs under a Bilateral Agreement for Joint Army Training and Exercises. The 14th edition (Jodhpur, 28 Jul–3 Aug 2025) included a command post exercise and professional exchanges. It is a model for a long-running exercise with a large Asian non-ally.

Singapore and Sweden amended their Defence Technology MOU in Nov 2024 to add defence innovation with start-ups, SMEs and universities. MINDEF says the collaboration has contributed to Singapore's protective infrastructure, submarines and surface vessels. It is a model for turning a technology framework, like the 2023 Japan agreement, into projects.

Changi RHCC co-organised Exercise COORES 2025 with Vietnam's VINASARCOM and US INDOPACOM's disaster-management centre. It drew 250 personnel from 39 militaries and 37 civil organisations and rehearsed a Vietnam-led Multinational Coordination Centre. It is a model for bringing the JSDF into RHCC-led HADR work.

signals.headline: Defense of Japan 2026 white paper names China the primary concern among China, North Korea and Russia. It puts drones and domestic defence production at the centre of the build-up.
signals.sowhat: Sets the official threat picture and priorities the SAF will hear in Japanese briefings this year.

signals.headline: MOD requests a record ¥8.89 trillion (about US$55.6B) for FY2027, prioritising unmanned systems, AI, long-range strike, air and missile defence, space and cyber.
signals.sowhat: Shows where Japanese money and industry will go in 2027. Drones and stand-off fires are also the SAF's main learning areas.

signals.headline: PM Takaichi reshuffles her cabinet on 17 September and keeps Defence Minister Koizumi Shinjiro to lead the security-document rewrite.
signals.sowhat: Continuity: Koizumi remains the ministerial counterpart through the strategy revision.

signals.headline: Active cyber defence operations begin on 1 October. In serious cases the SDF and police may access and neutralise servers used in attacks.
signals.sowhat: A new legal model for peacetime cyber defence that is worth studying alongside Singapore's own arrangements.

signals.headline: The Type 25 long-range anti-ship missile is shown to Kumamoto residents on 3 October, its first public display since deployment.
signals.sowhat: Japan is working to win local consent for counterstrike basing. It is a case study in explaining sensitive deployments to communities.

signals.headline: Keen Sword 2026 (19-29 October) rehearses Southwest Islands defence. US Marines will bring NMESIS and MADIS to Yonaguni for the first time.
signals.sowhat: The alliance's distributed sea-denial concept in practice. Watch for lessons on island logistics and dispersal.

Camp Fuji, near Gotemba (Type 25 glide weapon)

frame.question: What can the SAF learn from how Japan is turning a defence-only force into a joint force with long-range strike, unmanned systems and cyber powers while its recruit pool shrinks, and where are the practical openings to engage?
want: How the JSDF is reorganising for joint operations: the JJOC, the Ground Component Command, and the 15th Division in the Southwest Islands.
How Japan fields, bases and governs long-range counterstrike missiles within its legal limits and with local consent.
How Japan plans to use drones and AI at scale (SHIELD) to offset a shortage of people, and what it is learning from Ukraine.
What has worked in reversing the recruitment slide (pay, allowances, careers, women) as the youth cohort shrinks. This bears directly on the SAF's own demographic outlook.
What the end-2026 rewrite of the three security documents changes, plus named counterparts and venues for SAF engagement.
dont_want: A shopping list. Japan's purchases answer a different threat, scale and budget.
Treating Japan as a US proxy. Its choices also have their own legal, political and industrial drivers.
Taking sides in Japan's disputes with China, Korea or Russia, or framing engagement as alignment against any third country.
Anything beyond open sources, or exchanges that need classified access to be useful.
Planning on 2022-era assumptions. Strategy, budget and command structure are all changing in 2025-2026.

personnel.counts: Actual SDF uniformed strength at 31 March 2023 (2023 white paper, as reported); 92.2% of the 247,154 authorised
Actual SDF uniformed strength at 31 March 2025 (MOD): GSDF 131,293, MSDF 41,818, ASDF 42,608, Joint Staff etc. 4,533
Actual SDF uniformed strength at 31 March 2026 (MOD): GSDF 129,176, MSDF 41,463, ASDF 42,324, Joint Staff etc. 4,738

personnel_targets.text: Authorised (budgeted) uniformed strength is 247,154, almost unchanged for a decade. At 31 March 2026 only 88.1% was filled: GSDF 86.5%, MSDF 91.2%, ASDF 89.8%, Joint Staff etc. 91.9%.

Within the fixed ceiling, posts are shifting away from the GSDF. GSDF authorised strength fell from 150,500 (2023) to 149,403 (2026), while joint organisations rose from 4,367 to 5,158 and the ASDF from 46,994 to 47,131.
FY2023 recruiting hit a record low of 9,959 against a plan of 19,598 (51%). Only 30% of fixed-term 'SDF candidate' places were filled (3,221 of 10,628).
FY2024 recruiting was 9,724 (65% of plan), the second straight year below 10,000.

FY2025 recruiting recovered to 11,177 (+1,453, +14.9%), the first year above 10,000 in three years. General NCO-candidate intake rose for the first time in five years, to 4,946. Defence Minister Koizumi credits the new pay and allowances.

In December 2024 the government adopted a basic policy on SDF personnel. It creates more than 30 new allowances, raises pay, reviews the pay schedule and reviews raising retirement ages by about two years after FY2028.
An MOD plan (Nov 2024) abolishes the fixed-term 'SDF candidate' status and raises recruits' starting pay from ¥157,000 to ¥198,800 a month.
In Dec 2025 the overhaul of the SDF pay scale was brought forward to FY2027.
MOD projects the recruitable-age population to shrink by about 30% between FY2024 and FY2045.
The fill rate fell from 94.1% at end-FY2020 to 89.1% at end-FY2024, and the government is weighing a new agency to support retired SDF members (Aug 2026).

conops.text: Japan set up its National Security Council on 4 Dec 2013 and on 17 Dec adopted its first National Security Strategy. The strategy makes the NSC the 'control tower' of security policy, under a 'proactive contribution to peace based on the principle of international cooperation'.
conops.headline: First NSS, with NSC in charge

conops.text: The Abe cabinet decided to develop 'seamless' security legislation and reinterpreted the constitution to allow limited exercise of the right of collective self-defence, breaking with the post-war interpretation that had barred it.
conops.headline: Cabinet allows limited collective self-defence

conops.text: The Diet enacted the Legislation for Peace and Security, which put the 2014 decision into law. It took effect in March 2016.
conops.headline: Peace and security laws enacted

conops.text: The GSDF formed the Amphibious Rapid Deployment Brigade (planned at about 2,100 personnel) and the Ground Component Command. The brigade is a marine-type force built to land on, retake and secure remote islands.
conops.headline: Amphibious brigade stood up for islands

conops.text: New guidelines for FY2019 onward, with a FY2019-23 build-up plan, set the goal of a 'Multi-Domain Defense Force' that fuses space, cyber and electromagnetic capabilities with land, sea and air. They replace the 2013 'Dynamic Joint Defense Force' concept.
conops.headline: NDPG sets a Multi-Domain Defense Force
Extra budget drives biggest rise since 1972
conops.text: About $7bn of supplementary funding, added after the FY2021 budget, lifted 2021 military spending 7.3% to $54.1bn, then Japan's largest annual rise since 1972.

conops.headline: Three strategy documents set 2% goal
conops.text: The National Security Council and cabinet adopted the new strategy documents, including the Defense Buildup Program. The NSS sets a target of 2% of GDP for defence and related outlays by FY2027, replacing the long-standing ~1% norm.

conops.headline: Largest budget jump since 1952
conops.text: The FY2023 SDF budget of ¥6.8 trillion (~$52bn) was 26% above 2022, the largest year-on-year nominal rise in planned military spending since at least 1952.

Japan signed for up to 400 Tomahawk cruise missiles (200 Block IV and 200 Block V; the US-approved estimate was about $2.35bn), for delivery in FY2025-27, a year earlier than first planned. The missiles are for the counterstrike capability set out in the 2022 documents. On 29 Jul 2026 the destroyer JS Chokai fired Japan's first Tomahawk in a US-supported Pacific exercise.
conops.headline: Tomahawk deal makes counterstrike real
Pay package to fix recruiting
conops.text: The government adopted a basic policy to strengthen the SDF's human base: more than 30 new allowances, higher pay and a review of the pay schedule and retirement ages.

The JSDF Joint Operations Command (JJOC) opened at the Ministry of Defense in Ichigaya, Tokyo, with about 240 personnel under its first commander, Gen. Nagumo Kenichiro. It centrally oversees the three services and coordinates operations with US forces. On 30 Mar 2025 the US began phase one of turning US Forces Japan into a joint force headquarters.
conops.headline: Joint Operations Command stood up
Takaichi brings 2% target forward
conops.text: In her first policy speech, PM Takaichi said she would reach the 2% goal in FY2025, two years early, using a supplementary budget.

conops.headline: 2% of GDP reached two years early
conops.text: A FY2025 supplementary budget added about ¥1.1 trillion for defence, taking total defence-related spending to about ¥11 trillion, above 2% of GDP. Defence Minister Koizumi said the NSS's 2% level had effectively been reached.

conops.headline: Record budget funds hypersonics and drones
conops.text: The cabinet approved a record FY2026 defence budget of about ¥9.04 trillion (+3.8%). It includes ¥192.7bn for hypersonic guided missiles and ground equipment, and about ¥100bn for 'SHIELD', a drone-based coastal-defence concept to stop an invading force.

conops.headline: Budget enacted late after snap election
conops.text: The Diet passed the FY2026 budget (¥122.3 trillion overall, defence ¥9.04 trillion) on 7 April 2026, after the 1 April start of the fiscal year. Kyodo, as cited, says this last happened 11 years earlier; the delay followed February's snap election.

conops.headline: Military burden highest since 1958
conops.text: SIPRI put Japan's 2025 military spending at $62.2bn, or 1.4% of GDP, the highest share since 1958. It attributes the rise to the build-up plan launched in 2022 and to concern over China and North Korea.

PM Takaichi attended the first meeting of an expert panel on revising the 2022 strategy documents. The panel is due to report around autumn, and the cabinet aims to approve new documents by the end of 2026. The size of the defence budget, SDF capabilities and a possible partial review of the three non-nuclear principles are on the agenda.
conops.headline: Review of strategy documents begins

relations.text: Japan and Australia signed a Reciprocal Access Agreement, Japan's first visiting-forces agreement with any country other than the US. It entered into force on 13 Aug 2023.
relations.headline: First reciprocal access deal, with Australia

relations.text: PMs Kishida and Sunak signed a Japan-UK RAA at the Tower of London. It entered into force on 15 Oct 2023.
relations.headline: UK becomes second RAA partner

relations.text: Japan created Official Security Assistance (OSA), a grant-aid channel for equipment to like-minded militaries, in FY2023 (which began in April 2023). First-year funding was about ¥2bn. The Philippines received the first grant (about ¥600m for coastal radars, handed over in Feb 2026), and Malaysia signed a ¥400m grant for rescue boats in Dec 2023.
relations.headline: Official Security Assistance launched

relations.text: At Camp David, President Biden, PM Kishida and President Yoon agreed the 'Spirit of Camp David': deeper trilateral defence cooperation and a commitment to consult on regional threats. A multi-year exercise plan followed, and the first 'Freedom Edge' exercise ran in June 2024.
relations.headline: Camp David launches trilateral cooperation

relations.text: Japan, the UK and Italy signed the convention creating the GCAP International Government Organisation, a year after their leaders launched the programme in December 2022. The aim is a next-generation fighter by 2035, with work shared by contribution. The UK hosts the headquarters and a Japanese official is the first chief executive. Japan's MOFA reports the convention entered into force on 10 Dec 2024.
relations.headline: GCAP treaty signed in Tokyo

relations.text: The cabinet allowed exports of licence-built finished weapons to the licensor's country, which cleared PAC-3 Patriot interceptors for the US (re-export needs Japan's consent). On 26 Mar 2024 it approved selling the GCAP fighter to third countries, with each sale needing its own cabinet decision and countries at war excluded.
relations.headline: Export rules loosened for Patriots, GCAP

relations.text: At the 2024 US-Japan '2+2', the allies announced that US Forces Japan would become a joint force headquarters, reporting to INDOPACOM and working with Japan's new Joint Operations Command. Washington began phase one on 30 Mar 2025. Analysts note that existing policy and structures still limit the upgrade.
relations.headline: Alliance command upgrade announced

relations.text: Japan and the Philippines signed an RAA in Manila, Japan's first with an ASEAN member. It entered into force on 11 Sep 2025, and an ACSA followed (signed 15 Jan 2026, in force 22 Aug 2026).
relations.headline: Philippines signs first ASEAN RAA

relations.text: The cabinet and NSC revised the Three Principles on Transfer of Defense Equipment. They scrapped the rule limiting exports to five non-combat categories (rescue, transport, warning, surveillance, minesweeping) and now sort exports into 'non-arms' and 'arms', including lethal items such as fighters and warships. Sales to a country at war are allowed in special circumstances.
relations.headline: Five-category export limit scrapped

budget.text: Up every year since 2022 and still climbing, but more slowly in the core budget. On SIPRI's measure, spending rose from $46.0bn (about 1.1% of GDP) in 2022 to $62.2bn (1.4%) in 2025, 61% above 2016 and the highest burden since 1958. Yen growth outpaces dollar growth because the yen has weakened. On Japan's wider definition, 2% of GDP was reached in FY2025 through a supplementary budget, two years early. The FY2026 initial budget is a record ¥9.04 trillion but grew only 3.8%, so expect further increases to come partly through supplementary budgets until a successor plan to the FY2023-27 programme is set.

personnel.text: The SDF is shrinking while its budget grows. Actual strength fell from 227,843 (Mar 2023) to 220,252 (Mar 2025) and 217,701 (Mar 2026), or 88.1% of an unchanged 247,154 ceiling. Recruiting bottomed in FY2023 at 51% of plan and recovered to 11,177 in FY2025 after the December 2024 pay reforms, but strength still fell that year. The recruitable population is projected to fall about 30% by FY2045, so people, not money, is the binding constraint.

conops.text: Since the December 2022 documents, the buildup has favoured long-range stand-off strike and unmanned systems. The FY2026 budget funds hypersonic guided missiles (¥192.7bn) and the drone-based 'SHIELD' coastal-defence concept (~¥100bn). This judgement rests mainly on budget documents. Doctrinal milestones (collective self-defence, the 2015 legislation, the Joint Operations Command, counterstrike deployments) were not verified in this pass.

relations.text: SIPRI reads part of Japan's spending growth as a hedge against uncertainty over US support. Japan still funds US-forces realignment inside its own defence budget, so expect the alliance to stay central while Japan builds more independent capacity. Ties with Australia, the UK, Italy, the Philippines and others were not verified in this pass.

relation.text: Japan's treaty ally. Japan's defence-related budget carries SACO and US-forces realignment costs, and SIPRI links part of Japan's recent spending rise to growing uncertainty over US support.

relation.text: Japan's closest security partner after the US. Australia was the first country after the US to get a visiting-forces deal with Japan (RAA signed 6 Jan 2022, in force 13 Aug 2023), and the 2007 security declaration was updated in October 2022. Australia then chose the upgraded Mogami frigate (Aug 2025) and on 18 Apr 2026 signed for the first three of up to 11 ships, Tokyo's most consequential arms sale since the 2014 export rules.

relation.text: Japan's leading European partner. The RAA (signed 11 Jan 2023, Japan's second, in force 15 Oct 2023) lets the two forces train on each other's soil, and GCAP commits both, with Italy, to a next-generation fighter by 2035. The GCAP agency (GIGO) is based in the UK and its first chief executive is Japanese.

relation.text: Tied to Japan mainly through GCAP. A 2017 agreement covers transfers of defence equipment and technology, and an ACSA signed in Rome in November 2024 lets the two forces exchange supplies including fuel and ammunition. Italy was Japan's eighth ACSA partner.

agreements.name: Agreement concerning the transfer of defence equipment and technology

Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement (ACSA)

relation.text: Japan's fastest-growing defence tie in Southeast Asia. The Philippines has Japan's first RAA with an ASEAN state (signed 8 Jul 2024, in force 11 Sep 2025) and its first ASEAN ACSA (signed 15 Jan 2026, in force 22 Aug 2026). It was also the first recipient of OSA: five coastal radars, funded in FY2023 and handed over in Feb 2026.

Reciprocal Access Agreement (in force 11 Sep 2025)
Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement (in force 22 Aug 2026)

relation.text: A strategic partner with a standing foreign-and-defence '2+2' (third round, New Delhi, 20 Aug 2024) and an ACSA signed on 9 Sep 2020. During Modi's Aug 2025 visit to Tokyo the 2008 security declaration was revised to add economic security, the defence industry and cyber.

agreements.name: Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation
Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement
Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation (revised)

relation.text: Improving but still thinly institutionalised. The August 2023 Camp David summit set up regular US-Japan-ROK security cooperation, and the first multi-domain 'Freedom Edge' exercise followed in June 2024. Defence ministers met twice in 2026 (Yokosuka, 30 Jan; Seoul, 28 Jun), agreeing to work on AI and unmanned systems and to revive joint search-and-rescue drills. A bilateral ACSA was not a central item.

agreements.name: Spirit of Camp David (trilateral, with the US)

relation.text: A diplomatic grouping, not a defence pact. India was due to host the leaders' summit in 2025 but it has not taken place. Foreign ministers met in New Delhi in May 2026, and in September 2026 officials agreed only to keep working towards a summit, which Jiji judged unlikely soon because of US-India strains.
