scholars.name: Adam P. Liff
scholars.affiliation: Indiana University, Hamilton Lugar School of Global and International Studies - Associate Professor of East Asian International Relations; Nonresident Senior Fellow, Brookings Institution (Brookings-hosted CV dated Oct 2026)
focus: Japan's 2022 strategy documents and their implementation
Domestic politics of Japanese defence policy
US-Japan and US-ROK alliances in a Taiwan contingency

works.title: Kishida the Accelerator: Japan's Defense Evolution After Abe (The Washington Quarterly 46:1; summary page)
Myth vs. Reality in Japan's Historic Defense Transformation: Bringing the Domestic Politics Back In (public talk)

scholars.takeaway: Treats the December 2022 pledges (a much larger budget and long-range strike) as real but not a done deal: delivery depends on domestic politics and money. In Nov 2025 he warned that mistranslations of PM Takaichi's Taiwan remarks had generated more heat than light.

scholars.name: Sheila A. Smith
scholars.affiliation: Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), Washington - John E. Merow Senior Fellow for Asia-Pacific Studies
focus: The politics of Japan's military power

works.title: Understanding Takaichi Sanae (CFR conversation with Dr Sheila Smith)

scholars.takeaway: Reads PM Takaichi's security, defence and foreign policy as close to Abe's, with conservative support resting on a strong defence-spending line. Author of 'Japan Rearmed: The Politics of Military Power', a standard reference on how Japanese politics shapes the SDF.

scholars.name: Jeffrey W. Hornung
scholars.affiliation: RAND Corporation - Japan Lead, National Security Research Division
focus: Basing and new capabilities in Japan

works.title: Not Always Easy: Lessons Learned on Introducing New Defense Capabilities in Japan
Japan's Play for Today: Too Much? Just Right? Or Never Enough?

scholars.takeaway: Ten case studies of new US and Japanese capabilities and bases show that deploying new systems in Japan rarely goes smoothly. Planners should expect local and political friction and build time for it.

scholars.name: Christopher W. Hughes
scholars.affiliation: University of Warwick, Department of Politics and International Studies - Professor

works.title: Japan's 'three national security documents' and defense capabilities: reinforcing a radical military trajectory (Journal of Japanese Studies 50:1; listed on WRAP)
Japan's defence industrial strategy and fighter aircraft production: striving for tier-one status and the GCAP Project (Defence Studies 25:2; listed on staff page)

scholars.takeaway: Argues that the 2022 documents reinforce a radical shift towards a more capable military power closely integrated with the US. GCAP is Japan's bid for tier-one status in combat-aircraft production.

scholars.name: Koga Kei
scholars.affiliation: Nanyang Technological University (NTU), School of Social Sciences, Singapore - Associate Professor; Head of Division, Public Policy and Global Affairs
focus: Japan's grand strategy and Indo-Pacific policy
ASEAN, the Quad and regional institutions

works.title: Japan's Grand Strategy: Liminal Power in an Uncertain World (with Saori Katada; book launch notice)
Japan's Grand Strategy Amid Geopolitical Flux (podcast)

scholars.takeaway: Singapore-based. Reads Japan's Indo-Pacific strategy as long-run institutional adaptation, not just a reaction to China. He also tracks where the Quad and the US-Japan alliance are heading, which makes him a natural local guide for SAF commanders.

scholars.name: Sarah Soh
scholars.affiliation: S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), NTU, Singapore - Associate Research Fellow, Regional Security Architecture Programme

works.title: A Proactive Japan Deepens Pragmatic Cooperation with Southeast Asia (IDSS Paper IP26071)

scholars.takeaway: A Singapore-based analyst who follows how Tokyo's security outreach lands in Southeast Asia, and an easy contact for IREO. Only the title of her 2026 paper was captured.

scholars.name: John F. Bradford
scholars.affiliation: RSIS, Singapore - Adjunct Senior Fellow, Maritime Security Programme; Executive Director, Yokosuka Council on Asia-Pacific Studies (YCAPS)

works.title: Japan's Official Security Assistance to Southeast Asia: Limited Scope, but Real Impact (IDSS Paper IP25005; with Raymond Yamamoto)

scholars.takeaway: A retired US Navy commander and former Country Director for Japan in the Office of the Secretary of Defense. He finds OSA small (¥2bn in its first year) but with a real effect on military cooperation in Southeast Asia, and he studies why Japan-ASEAN defence ties have moved slowly.

SPF IINA column on why Japan's defence spending is set 'amount-first' (Japanese; exact title not captured)

scholars.takeaway: Japan's main bridge to European and NATO thinking. He served as Advisor for NATO at Japan's Embassy in Belgium (2005-08) and is a useful voice on how Tokyo links European and Indo-Pacific security.

scholars.takeaway: An Australian specialist on Japan-Australia security ties who follows US-Japan-Australia trilateralism and smaller 'minilateral' groupings closely. His 2025 book is Strategic Minilateralism in the Indo-Pacific.

items.text: After winning a two-thirds lower-house majority on 8 February 2026, PM Takaichi's government is rewriting the 2022 National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy and Defense Buildup Program for approval by the end of 2026. On the table: how much to spend and how to pay, drones and AI, the defence industry, the non-nuclear principles and nuclear-powered submarines. Defence Minister Koizumi was kept on to lead it.
items.headline: Rewriting the strategy

items.text: Defence and related spending reached about ¥11 trillion in FY2025, which Japan counts as 2% of GDP, two years early. The FY2026 MOD budget is a record ¥9.04 trillion, and Washington is pressing for 3.5%.
items.headline: Record budgets, 2% hit early

items.text: On 31 March 2026 the GSDF fielded Japan's first long-range missiles: the Type 25 anti-ship missile (about 1,000 km) and the Type 25 glide weapon. The destroyer Chokai fired Japan's first Tomahawk on 29 July 2026.
items.headline: Counterstrike missiles now fielded

items.text: The JJOC has commanded all three services in operations since March 2025. The 15th Brigade on Okinawa is due to become a division within FY2026. Keen Sword (19–29 October 2026) rehearses multi-island sea denial, with US Marine anti-ship missiles on Yonaguni for the first time.
items.headline: Joint command, southwest focus

items.text: Unmanned at scale: ¥100.1 billion in FY2026 for SHIELD, a layered coastal drone defence due by FY2027, and 17 MQ-9B SeaGuardians in the FY2027 request. Since 1 October 2026 the SDF and police can neutralise attacking servers under the active cyber defence law.
items.headline: Drones, AI and active cyber

items.text: The SDF is at about 89% of its authorised 247,154. Hiring rose about 15% to 11,177 in FY2025 after pay reforms but stayed below target, and MOD expects the recruitable population to shrink about 30% by FY2045.

talking_points.context: For a first conversation with a JSDF counterpart (Joint Staff, JJOC or a service staff office), for example on the sidelines of the Shangri-La Dialogue or during a visit to Tokyo in the 60th-anniversary year.

points.text: Mark 60 years of diplomatic relations (26 April 1966) and the Strategic Partnership the two Prime Ministers announced in March 2026.
points.why: A shared milestone that frames the conversation as part of a leader-level commitment.

points.text: Thank the JMSDF for hosting RSS Steadfast and the first Exercise Singapan in August 2026, and recall Gen. Uchikura's Singapore visit that month.
points.why: Opens on the most recent, concrete activity between the two forces.

points.text: What has the Joint Operations Command changed in practice since March 2025, and what would you do differently standing it up today?
points.why: JJOC is the SDF's main command reform, and its early lessons are directly useful to an integrated SAF.

points.text: Which recruiting measures made the FY2025 difference, and which labour-saving steps (automation, lean crews) are you counting on?
points.why: Shrinking intakes are the problem both forces share most, and it invites an honest exchange.

points.text: How will the SDF train and sustain several thousand SHIELD drones by the end of FY2027?
points.why: Mirrors the SAF's own push to put drones in every unit.

points.text: After Noto, how do you hand over from rescue to months of life support, and how should foreign militaries plug in?
points.why: Japan has the deepest large-scale disaster experience in the region, and the question opens the RHCC offer.

points.text: Changi RHCC's coordination experience, which JSDF personnel used at RIMPAC 2026, and a place for JSDF planners at the next Exercise COORES.
points.why: Practical, low-cost and already tested together.

points.text: How the RSN runs autonomous MARSEC USVs with two-person crews in the Singapore Strait, as a start on the lean-manning exchanges the Partnership names.
points.why: Gives Japan something concrete in return, in the partnership's own terms.

points.text: Singapore's role as ASEAN–Japan coordinator to 2027 and incoming ASEAN chair, to help shape Japan's ASEAN defence agenda.
points.why: Plays to Singapore's convening strength. Japan was not among GUIDE's 17 founding endorsers.

points.text: Do not raise Japan's constitutional debate (Article 9), wartime history or Japanese domestic politics.
points.why: These are sensitive in Japan and the region, are not Singapore's business, and could derail a first call. Singapore's own readouts keep to cooperation and regional developments.

points.text: Do not frame cooperation against any third country. Singapore speaks of regional peace, stability and a rules-based order.
points.why: This is Singapore's long-standing position, and it keeps the channel professional.

points.text: Do not imply Singapore will buy equipment under the 2023 transfer agreement or Japan's 2026 export changes; the agreement obliges neither side.
points.why: Avoids raising industry expectations and media speculation.
